headline: Banks split on day one of earnings (Goldman and Citi beat, JPMorgan missed on both lines), UnitedHealth and J&J raised guidance, and the memory chip selloff turned into a rout with Korea's KOSPI down about 6% below 6,000.
summary: Earnings season opened with a split. Goldman earned $17.01 a share against roughly $13 expected on a 72% jump in equities trading, and Citi beat too, but JPMorgan missed on both earnings and revenue for a rare time as expenses rose 12%, and the stock was down about 3.5% before the open. In health care, UnitedHealth beat and raised its full year outlook to at least $20.50 a share as its medical cost ratio fell to 88.4%, and J&J raised its 2026 sales outlook to about $101.2 billion. Overnight the memory chip selloff deepened: the KOSPI fell about 6% and broke below 6,000, SK Hynix fell about 8.5%, Taiwan fell about 2% with near record foreign selling, and Kioxia fell 13% in Tokyo. Oil is a little softer this morning, with Brent near $105.50 after settling at $106.65 on Monday, and the 10 year yield eased to about 5.19% as bonds reopened. S&P 500 futures are flat and Nasdaq futures about 0.5% lower, so no setup is close to a confirmed breakout before Wednesday's CPI.

regime.why: Banks show credit is fine (JPMorgan's loss provisions fell 19%) and trading desks are booming, but the AI chip trade is cracking where it is most crowded: memory and optics. Oil above $100 and a 5.2% 10 year yield into Wednesday's CPI keep the inflation risk alive. Normal size only on breakouts that confirm on 1.5x volume; stay out of memory and wait for TSMC on Thursday before adding AI chip exposure.

signals.title: Banks split: Goldman and Citi beat, JPMorgan misses on both lines and Wells Fargo misses on revenue
signals.what_happened: JPMorgan reported Q3 earnings of $5.57 a share against a FactSet estimate of $5.93, and revenue of $50.17 billion against $51.23 billion (MarketScreener). Net interest income rose 13% to $27.1 billion, but expenses rose 12% to $27.3 billion, and Dimon said trading and banking activity 'did moderate somewhat'. Loss provisions fell 19% to $2.7 billion and the dividend goes up about 10% to $1.65. The stock was down about 3.5% premarket. Goldman earned $17.01 a share against about $12.86 to $13.08 expected, on revenue of $18.68 billion, up 23%, with equities trading up 72% to $6.44 billion; it was up about 3.5% premarket. Citi earned $2.85 against $2.62 expected on revenue of $23.85 billion, up 8%, but slipped about 1% premarket. Wells Fargo earned $1.87 against $1.85 but revenue of $21.87 billion missed the $22.31 billion estimate, and it was down 1% to 2% premarket.
signals.so_what: The money is in trading, not lending. Volatile markets and high rates pay trading desks (Goldman, and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday), while big balance sheet lenders are paying more to run the bank. Credit is not the problem: provisions fell. Second order: if JPMorgan's costs keep rising faster than revenue, the whole group's earnings estimates drift down even with a strong economy. Third order: exchanges and market makers (CBOE, NDAQ, HOOD) earn from the same volatility that helped Goldman. What would make this wrong: Bank of America and Morgan Stanley on Wednesday show the same cost squeeze without the trading offset.
signals.for_you: Long term: JPM and C are both 'Buy zone now' on the dashboard, but JPM was already down 5.7% over a month, so a 3% drop today would trip the 'not down more than 8% in a month' check; do not buy JPM today and let the rating update tonight. C beat and is the cleaner one: new put idea C $122 (bottom of its buy zone, about 7.5% under Monday's close; see Setups for the live quote). Swing: no bank is a swing setup. If you sell puts, wait until BAC and MS report Wednesday before adding more financials.

signals.title: UnitedHealth beats and raises for the third time; J&J lifts its 2026 sales and profit outlook
signals.what_happened: UnitedHealth earned $4.69 a share adjusted on revenue of $112.7 billion and raised its 2026 outlook to at least $20.50 a share, from $19.50 to $20.00, above the $19.87 consensus (SEC 8-K, GuruFocus). Its medical care ratio, the share of premiums paid out for care, fell to 88.4% from 89.9% a year ago, and the operating cost ratio fell to 12.8% from 13.5%. The stock was up about 2.5% to 4% premarket. J&J sales rose 5.9% to $25.4 billion and adjusted EPS was $2.59 against about $2.51 to $2.53 expected; it raised 2026 sales guidance to about $101.2 billion and adjusted EPS to $11.10 at the midpoints. GAAP EPS was only $0.09 because of a one time charge for the proposed talc settlement.
signals.so_what: UnitedHealth is getting its pricing power back: it raised premiums and trimmed benefits, so each premium dollar pays out less in care. Who pays: Medicare Advantage members and employers. Who gets paid: insurers first (UNH, and by read across CI and CVS). Second order for medtech: a falling care ratio can mean insurers are pushing back harder on procedures, so watch whether hospital volume names like ISRG and SYK talk about it when they report. Third order: J&J crossing $100 billion in sales with a talc deal in sight removes its biggest legal overhang. What would make this wrong: the drop in the care ratio came from one time reserve releases rather than lasting pricing.
signals.for_you: Swing: UNH is not a dashboard swing setup; its up/down volume is 0.78 (distribution) and it is down 10.4% over 3 months, so a gap up on news is not a trade until volume turns. Puts: UNH and JNJ were on your MT Put Candidates list Monday; now that the numbers are out, wait for the opening gap to hold a day before selling puts (see Setups for live quotes). Long term: JNJ is rated Wait and CI and CVS are 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' (both fail the up/down volume check), so no buys yet; this news could help those charts repair.

signals.title: Memory chip selloff becomes a rout: KOSPI down about 6% below 6,000, SK Hynix about -8.5%, Taiwan and Tokyo chip stocks hit
signals.since_yesterday: The KOSPI fell another ~6% on Oct 13 and broke below 6,000 with a sell sidecar, after Micron closed down 3.88% at $989.04 Monday and the SOX fell about 2.7%.
signals.what_happened: Korea's KOSPI fell more than 6% intraday on Oct 13 and broke below 6,000, triggering a sell sidecar at 9:47am, the first in about two months (SBS, Seoul Economic Daily). SK Hynix traded about 8.5% lower near 1.47 million won and Samsung about 6.8% lower near 233,500 won. In the US on Monday, Micron closed down 3.88% at $989.04 and every stock in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell, with the index down about 2.7% (Motley Fool, 24/7 Wall St.). China's CXMT said it expects to launch DDR5 server memory on a denser 4F2 cell design around the end of 2026; TrendForce puts its DRAM share at 9.5% in Q2 against Micron's 23.3%. The Wall Street Journal says CXMT is still two to three generations behind. Taiwan's Taiex fell 1.95% to 48,341 with NT$165 billion of foreign selling, the third largest on record, and Tokyo's Nikkei fell about 1.7% to 1.8% as Kioxia dropped 13% and Tokyo Electron 7%.
signals.so_what: Memory is a commodity. Its prices and profits peak when everyone has built capacity at once, and investors sell before the price drop shows up in earnings. CXMT does not need to match Samsung; it only needs to add enough server memory to end the shortage. Who gets paid: buyers of memory (cloud companies, PC and phone makers) if prices ease. Who gets hurt: memory makers and the tool makers they buy from (LRCX, AMAT). Third order: when a crowded trade unwinds, foreign funds sell what they can, so Taiwan and Japan fall too even though TSMC's sales are still up over 50%. What would make this wrong: TSMC on Thursday and Micron's own guidance show demand still running ahead of supply into 2027.
signals.for_you: Swing: skip memory and chip equipment swings until the selling stops; no dashboard swing setup is a memory name. Long term: LRCX is 'Buy zone now' (up 3.9% over a month even after Monday's 2.9% drop), but memory makers are big customers, so wait until after TSMC's Thursday report before adding. AMAT stays 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' (up/down volume 0.84). If you sell puts, chip premiums are rich now, but only on names you would own through another 20% drop.

signals.title: Optics stocks drop on profit taking: Lumentum -9.8%, Coherent -7.9%, Arista -2.7%
signals.what_happened: On Monday Lumentum fell 9.8% to $995.41 on 1.35x normal volume, Coherent fell 7.9% to $288.02 on about normal volume, and Arista fell 2.7% to $210.88 on light volume (dashboard data, Oct 12 close). Reports point to profit taking after big gains, a 'sell the news' reaction to optical demos at the OCP Global Summit, and a Lumentum CFO stock sale on Oct 1, not to any change in demand; the same coverage says Lumentum's component capacity is sold out into early 2029 (Yahoo Finance). The cause is not confirmed by the companies.
signals.so_what: Yesterday the money looked like it was rotating from memory into optics. Monday says the whole AI hardware group is being trimmed together, which is what happens when rates are above 5% and the trade is crowded. Optics demand is tied to AI cluster build outs, which are still growing, so this looks like positioning, not fundamentals. What would make this wrong: TSMC or the cloud companies cut 2027 capex plans.

signals.title: Oil follow up: Brent settles at $106.65, Ukraine pauses refinery strikes but Russia keeps hitting Ukraine's grid
signals.since_yesterday: Brent settled at $106.65 and WTI rose 2.06% to $93.74 on Monday; Ukraine has held off refinery strikes for two days while Russia hit six energy sites on Oct 12.
signals.what_happened: WTI settled up 2.06% at $93.74 and Brent at $106.65 on Monday, and Brent was about 1% lower near $105.50 early Tuesday (TechFlow, CoinCentral). Ukraine has not struck Russian refineries for two days since Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim, but Russia hit six Ukrainian energy sites on Oct 12, injuring 33, and Naftogaz said gas facilities in Kharkiv were attacked overnight (Moscow Times, Kyiv Independent). The Kremlin says talks continue. Zelensky wants the deal to cover the power grid, not just oil. Near Hormuz, UKMTO reported a crude tanker hit by an unknown projectile on Oct 11 and a product tanker on Oct 12 (CBS live updates).
signals.so_what: A one sided pause helps Russia: its refineries get a rest while Ukraine's grid keeps getting hit, so this pause is unlikely to last. Fewer Ukrainian strikes means more Russian diesel exports, which is why diesel has eased more than crude. Crude itself is still set by Hormuz, where tankers are still being hit. What would make this wrong: a signed deal covering both oil and power, plus a Hormuz reopening.
signals.for_you: Swing: XOM closed at 172.15, just 0.4% under its 172.91 pivot, but Monday volume was 0.65x normal; it needs 20.4M+ shares on the breakout day. A news outlet called the oil majors breakouts on Monday, but by the dashboard rule none confirmed. COP (new on Setups: entry 141.91, needs 10M+ shares, up/down 1.12, 20% ahead of SPY over 3 months) and CVX (entry 218.23, needs 12.8M+ shares, up/down 1.00, a flat month) are further away. Puts: no new energy put idea today.

cycle.quadrant_why: Growth: banks reported strong activity, with JPMorgan's net interest income up 13% and Goldman's revenue up 23%, and JPMorgan's loss provisions fell 19%, so credit is not cracking. Inflation: Brent settled at $106.65 Monday and September CPI on Wednesday is expected around 3.6% to 3.7% a year, up from 3.4% (consensus cited in Monday's brief). In Dalio's four seasons this is still rising inflation with steady growth.
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Late, and tightening is now global. The Fed is at 3.75% to 4.00%, the US 10 year is about 5.19%, India's RBI raised to 5.50% and is defending a rupee near record lows, and Korea's central bank has hiked twice. Late cycle tightening shows up first in the most crowded, most foreign owned trades, which is exactly where today's selling is: Korean and Taiwanese chips.
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. Debt is high and long rates are above 5%. Dalio warned last week that China and Japan may buy fewer Treasuries and that the US could face a debt crisis within three years. When the biggest buyers of government debt step back, long rates stay high even if the Fed stops hiking.
cycle.big_cycle: Four of the five forces are active. Debt and money: high debt, 5% long rates. Internal order: a split US three weeks before the Nov 3 midterms. External order: the Gulf war (tankers still hit near Hormuz), a Russia Ukraine 'ceasefire' only one side is keeping, and US China rivalry now in memory chips. Technology: the AI build out, still the main tailwind, but its most crowded parts are being sold.
tailwinds: Trading desks and exchanges are earning record fees from volatility (Goldman equities +72%).
Health insurers have regained pricing (UnitedHealth's care ratio down to 88.4%).
TSMC's sales are still growing over 50% a year.
headwinds: Memory chips are in a classic cycle top scare as China adds supply.
A 5.2% 10 year yield and $105 oil into CPI.
Bank costs rising faster than revenue at the biggest lender.

history.what: DRAM prices peaked in Q3 2018 and roughly halved within months. Micron fell a little more than 50% from its 2018 peak to its low and ended the year down 22.8%, even though its earnings were near records when the slide began.
history.lesson: Memory stocks fall before memory profits do. The stock bottomed a few months after earnings peaked, not when the news got bad.

source.title: Why Micron Technology stock fell 22.8% in 2018 (Motley Fool, Jan 14, 2019)

history.what: Oil quadrupled and inflation surged. The S&P 500 fell about 48% from its January 1973 high to the October 1974 low, and even Exxon and Chevron fell about 44%.
history.lesson: In a true oil shock with rising inflation, almost nothing is safe. Cash and short duration held up best.

source.title: Museum of American Finance: 1970s Bear Market

history.what: The S&P 500 lost about 19% for the year and entered a bear market in June, while the energy sector returned more than 60%, the best sector by far.
history.lesson: In the rising inflation season, energy and real assets lead and long duration growth lags.

source.title: Investing Daily: The Leaders and Laggards of 2022

cycle.differences: The 2018 memory comparison replaces the 1990 Gulf War today because the setup changed: the biggest move is now a chip cycle scare, not a war shock. What is different from 2018: AI servers are a new, growing source of memory demand, and CXMT is still two to three generations behind the leaders, so the supply wave may be smaller. What is the same: the stocks were priced for peak profits, and foreign money is leaving fast.
cycle.for_you: Swing: favor setups outside chips that confirm on volume (energy, ZBRA, PFE, GILD); skip memory and wait for TSMC before any AI hardware entry. Puts: sell only where you would own the stock through a 20% drop; C at $122 and PFE at $27 fit, chip names do not yet. Long term: buy quality in tranches, and treat 'Buy zone now' names that are falling fast (JPM, COHR) as wait until the next rating update.

principle.applied: The memory rout hurts, and the useful part is the lesson: memory is a cycle, and the stocks top when profits look best. Write down your rule now (no memory swings until the selling stops and volume turns up), so the next time a commodity chip stock looks cheap after a big run, you already know what to do.
